cards.title: ChatGPT is adding real cartoonists' signatures to fake New Yorker cartoons

depth.text: someone found ChatGPT putting **real cartoonists’ signatures** on **fake New Yorker cartoons**

The reporter documented **more than 15 New Yorker cartoonists** whose signatures the image generator used without permission or compensation. Even after OpenAI was alerted, ChatGPT **still signed** some generated cartoons with real cartoonists’ names.

cards.title: Dust: Pretraining Transformers Without Backpropagation

depth.text: someone trained **transformer language models** **without backprop** by perturbing activations at each token
A **243M-parameter model** beat one **120× smaller** at most population sizes. The authors say Dust isn’t compute-efficient enough to replace backprop today.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics say derivative-free methods are costly and unlikely to matter; others see promise in their generality and the finding that larger models can be more population-efficient.

comments.text: Every few years, a derivative-free neural network optimization algorithm gets some hype. I'd bet my life savings that none of them ever make an impact. Derivative-free optimization can be useful for genuinely discontinuous objectives [1], but common neural network objectives are smooth and/or Lipschitz. The gradient is useful. Instead of trying random directions and hoping that one of them is an…

I'm skeptical as to whether zeroth-order methods really lend themselves to a Bitter Lesson argument. First-order methods don't explore the loss landscape optimally, but the loss function tends to be nonconvex, and zeroth-order methods don't address that issue head on. Dust smooths, and so do applicable first-order methods. Remove the nonconvexity issue, and I suspect Dust's purported advantages…

> There are many interesting open questions. The first is whether, and how, Dust can find better directions than backprop’s first-order gradient Both algorithms are bound by the same Pareto frontier based on the Empirical Risk Minimisation Principle, so they’re already on the same trajectory.
Interestingly backprop is limited by conditioning of the Hessian matrix in order to converge…

Even though this is way more expensive than backprop, could a hybrid approach where you fine tune an existing checkpoint that's been backpropped unlock further gains?
It would be cool to apply this to different stages and see if that affects the learning trajectory
It's computationally expensive and infeasible but what's the upside? Genuine question due to unfamiliarity with the subject.

cards.title: The technology to eradicate mosquito-borne disease exists

depth.text: someone says the US could **wipe out mosquito-borne diseases**, but **regulators have held up the tools**

Oxitec’s **engineered male Aedes aegypti** pass on a gene that kills female offspring; field trials cut wild populations by **80 percent** in the Cayman Islands and about 95 percent in Brazil. Years of **regulatory delays** held up Oxitec’s US rollout, while MosquitoMate received full nationwide commercial registration for its Wolbachia mosquitoes in April 2024.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters want disease-carrying mosquitoes eradicated; critics worry removing them could harm ecosystems and eliminate a food source.

cards.title: Mold Linker Version 3.0.0 Release – Rewritten in Rust

depth.text: mold's first **Rust release** replaces C++ without slowing down **linking**

It’s meant as a **drop-in replacement** for 2.42.1, with the same command-line options, target architectures, and output apart from listed bug fixes. For corrupted input, reads are now **bounds-checked**, so mold stops with a panic at the faulty access rather than the old C++ version’s out-of-bounds reads and segmentation fault. Building it now uses **Cargo**, requires Rust 1.95 or later, and a C compiler.

cards.camps: Two camps: one distro maintainer says they’ll have to keep a C version to bootstrap Rust; another commenter expects mold to be even better in Rust.

cards.title: Opus 5.5 agents discover two room-temperature magnetic semiconductor candidates

depth.text: someone's AI agents found two **magnetic semiconductor** candidates, including one material **first made in 1999**

**YBaMnFeO₅** is a designed candidate that may be hard to make; **KV[Cr(CN)₆]** was first made in 1999. Calculations for perfect crystals predict both are semiconductors with **zero net spin moment** and spin-sorted electrons. The older sample stayed magnetically ordered up to 376 K, but its band gap and spin sorting remain unmeasured.

The agents ran quantum-mechanical simulations of each crystal with the standard method for this, density functional theory, at two levels of approximation: a faster one (PBE+U) and a slower, usually more accurate one (HSE06). The band gaps and spin windows below come from the more accurate one.
So…

Okay? Aren't the semiconductors we use today room temperature? I certainly don't use helium to cool my phone. I don't see any claims that this is better than the current silicon and gallium arsenide semiconductors that we use. And the use of "room temperature" seems a deliberate attempt to misconstrue this with superconductors

cards.title: Plain text is still one of the best technologies we have

depth.text: someone makes the case that **plain text** stays **readable**, portable, and useful as software changes

The writer points to **text files** working across Linux, Windows, terminals, web servers, and programs, and their role in code, configuration, and logs. **Markdown** adds headings, lists, and links while keeping its source readable; the article says plain text is not right for every job.

cards.camps: Two camps: plain-text fans praise its durability and portability; skeptics point to encoding and line-ending problems, and one commenter argues agents make binary formats easier to recover.

comments.text: Graydon Hoare, the creator of the Rust programming language, wrote his seminal piece on text in 2014. In it, he said "text is the most powerful, useful, effective communication technology ever, period."[1] Text is durable. [1] https://archive.ph/FhG5L (the original either got deleted or login-walled, here is the archived version) [2] https://hn.algolia.com/?q=always+bet+on+text [3]…

The article briefly addresses the problem, but it's pretty fun how different "plain text" looks throughout history and in different domains. For one, there are a few different ways to terminate lines. All major operating systems now tend to use just 
, but I have older files that use 
 (Microsoft),  (Macintosh) or 
 (RiscOS). There are also different opinions on how text files end in…

This is the public dividend of a standard finally winning. The article gives credit to Unicode, but it is the fact that ASCII unambiguously won that gives plain text its portability and longevity. It looks like Unicode is on its way to winning in the same way, but it is not there yet. Most text files I write are still pure ASCII because that's the only way to avoid unexpected glitches [0]. [0]…

What, no mention of our old friend, ASCII-armored Base64? For shame! Everything can be text with Base64, including things that have absolutely no business being text! Best of all, in light of popular widespread abuse of every available resource, Base64 is comparatively efficient! Bring on the petabytes! Yay and I'm not being completely sarcastic

Fun timing on this plaintext conversation. I built a little browser based plaintext playwriting app this weekend for a little weekend project. Found myself really hating 1. how clunk screenwriting software can be and 2. How unsharable the files are. With plaintext you can hand the file off to anyone on any device--the caveat being absolutely no one wants to be handed a plaintext script. The…

cards.title: Qualcomm licenses patents on Huawei’s LogicFolding chip tech

depth.text: Qualcomm is **licensing patents** on Huawei's **LogicFolding chip tech**

One commenter relays a claim that **Huawei is getting net revenue** from Qualcomm, but says they don't know if it's true. Another quotes a statement that the transaction will close after **regulatory approvals**.

cards.camps: Some see cross-licensing as the only operational path; others call the patent system a cartel or rigged.

comments.text: A Chinese technology/military propagandist I follow asserted today that Huawei is getting net revenue from Qualcomm on this deal, marking a change from being a buyer/licensor of western technology to a provider. I don't know if it's true but this individual historically promotes the Chinese state view via selective presentation of facts rather than made-up claims.

Interesting. LogicFolding is something that seems so obvious in retrospect and yet somebody has to be the first to do it. I did find it neat that it ends up actually reducing overall heat despite the multiple layer wafers as signals have less overall distance to travel as they move in layer space rather than across the chip.
Aren't Huawei on the Entity List? How can Qualcomm enter into agreements like this without getting into massive hot water?
Will be interesting to see how Ericsson - if at all - responds to this
Remember when they were telling us how important the 5G race was and how critical was for the US to lead it? And now they are just giving it away ?
